name: Integrity: Process Over Detection
title: Integrity: Process Over Detection
answer: Integrity: Process Over Detection means schools should judge how a piece of writing was made rather than rely on software that guesses whether AI wrote it. Detection scores are unreliable, especially for students still learning English, so the safer path is to make the writing process visible through drafts, in-class work, conferences and marked AI use levels. This matters because it protects students from false accusations and teaches them that how they write is part of the work.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: Many schools first answered AI writing by buying detection software, but the book argues this is the wrong starting point. A widely cited study found that detection tools often flagged essays by writers whose first language is not English as machine written when they were not, meaning a student learning English could be accused of cheating for writing simply. Some detectors perform better, and one test company built detectors that showed no such bias on its own adult test data, but a school cannot easily know how its own tool behaves with its own students. The book's position is that a detection score should never be treated as proof of cheating, and at most it is a reason to look more closely at how a piece of writing was made. The idea solves the problem of false accusations by shifting attention from guessing at a finished product to examining the process that produced it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the book points to version history as a way to see how a piece of writing developed over time, and a draft that appears all at once deserves a conversation. Teachers can also use short writing done in class, brief conferences where students explain their choices, and AI use levels marked on each assignment, all of which make the student's own thinking visible. Figure 6.5 brings these elements together as a set. The text does not give separate grade band versions of this practice, so the same process focus applies across kindergarten through twelfth grade. This approach also changes the relationship between teachers and students, because instead of trying to catch students, teachers design work where the process is part of the grade.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research support and cites specific findings. A widely cited study found that tools built to detect AI writing often flagged essays by writers whose first language is not English as machine written when they were not (Liang et al., 2023). The text also notes that some detectors perform better, and one test company built detectors that showed no such bias on its own adult test data (Jiang et al., 2024). However, the book cautions that a school cannot easily know how its own tool behaves with its own students, and it repeats the point from Chapter 3 that a detection score should never be treated as proof of cheating. The evidence therefore supports caution about detection and supports process-based approaches as more reliable.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The book sets clear limits on detection tools. A detection score should never be treated as proof of cheating, and at most it is a reason to look more closely at how a piece of writing was made. The risk of false accusation is real, especially for students whose first language is not English, who may be flagged for writing simply. The decisions that stay with a person include how to read version history, when a draft that appears all at once deserves a conversation, how to run conferences where students explain their choices, and how to mark AI use levels on assignments. The text does not offer legal guidance, and it describes practice rather than rules, so schools must make their own judgments about how to apply these ideas with their own students.
